sections.section_title: Arming With Christ's Disposition Toward Suffering
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Christ's suffering in the flesh becomes the model for the community's own posture: they must arm themselves with the same mindset, choosing to endure suffering for faithfulness rather than reverting to former sinful patterns, thereby living for God's will rather than human desires.
sections.relevance: The passage presents the community's break with sin as an active human choice. The military metaphor 'arm yourselves' (hoplisasthe) is an imperative presupposing genuine agency. The one who 'has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin' not through an automatic mechanism but through 'the lived experience of choosing God's will over human desire when that choice costs something.' The contrast between living for 'human lusts' and 'the will of God' frames ongoing faithfulness as a genuine human decision with salvific implications.
key_phrases: arm yourselves also with the same purpose
the one who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin
no longer for human lusts, but for the will of God

sections.section_title: The Former Way of Life and the Astonishment of Former Companions
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies the community's former Gentile lifestyle of sensuality, drunkenness, and idolatry, and explains that the social hostility they now face is the backlash from former companions astonished by the community's break with those norms.

sections.section_title: Accountability and the Gospel Preached to the Dead
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that slanderers will give account to the divine judge of the living and the dead, and that the gospel was preached to believers who have since died so that, though they experienced death in the flesh like all humans, they might live in the spirit according to God, replicating Christ's own death-to-life pattern.
sections.relevance: The accountability language presupposes genuine human agency: the slanderers chose to malign the community and will answer for that choice. The verb apeitho (used of disobedience in the broader context, 4:17) describes active resistance to God's message, not inability imposed by divine decree. The dead believers heard the gospel during their lifetime and responded to it; their living 'in the spirit according to God' is the outcome of having received and responded to a proclamation, not of being unilaterally determined to receive it.
key_phrases: they will give account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead
the gospel has been preached even to those who are dead
they may live in the spirit according to God

sections.section_title: The Nearness of the End and the Priority of Love
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the nearness of the end generates imperatives for mental clarity, sobriety for prayer, and above all fervent mutual love that covers a multitude of sins and holds the community together under external pressure.

sections.section_title: Hospitality and the Stewardship of God's Varied Grace
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes the community's call to ungrudging hospitality and faithful stewardship of God's multifaceted grace-gifts, with all speaking and serving directed toward God's glorification through Jesus Christ.

sections.section_title: The Fiery Ordeal and Sharing in Christ's Sufferings
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the community's fiery ordeal is not something strange but a purposeful testing, and that to the degree the community shares Christ's sufferings it is to rejoice, because present sharing in suffering is the condition for sharing in future glory at the revelation of Christ.
sections.relevance: The testing presupposes genuine human response: the community must endure rather than abandon faithfulness, and must choose to rejoice rather than despair. The imperative 'keep on rejoicing' (chairete, present tense) commands a sustained posture that only genuine agents can adopt. The connection between present suffering and future glory is framed as contingent on participation: 'to the degree that you share the sufferings of Christ' implies that the degree of sharing is variable and depends on the community's own faithfulness under trial.
key_phrases: which comes upon you for your testing
to the degree that you share the sufferings of Christ, keep on rejoicing
at the revelation of His glory you may rejoice with exultation

sections.section_title: Suffering for the Name of Christ
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that being insulted for the name of Christ is blessed because the Spirit of glory rests upon those so insulted, but the blessedness applies only to suffering for Christ's name, not to suffering earned by criminal or meddlesome behavior; the community must therefore glorify God in the name 'Christian' rather than being ashamed.
sections.relevance: The passage draws a critical distinction between blessed and unblessed suffering that depends entirely on human choices. Whether one suffers as a Christian or as a murderer, thief, evildoer, or meddler is a matter of the person's own behavior. The imperative 'make sure that none of you suffers as a murderer' presupposes that the community can and must choose how it conducts itself. The blessedness is not automatic or decreed; it is contingent on suffering for the right reason, which is within human control.
key_phrases: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed
Make sure that none of you suffers as a murderer, or thief, or evildoer, or a troublesome meddler
if anyone suffers as a Christian, he is not to be ashamed, but is to glorify God in this name

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the community's suffering is the beginning of God's purifying judgment at his own household, and that if even the righteous are saved with difficulty through fiery testing, the outcome for those who actively disobey the gospel is incomparably worse.
sections.relevance: The verb apeithounton ('those who disobey') describes 'active resistance to God's message, not mere ignorance,' presenting disobedience as a genuine human choice with eschatological consequences. The a fortiori argument presupposes that both the righteous and the godless are responsible agents: the righteous endure the difficult path of faithfulness, while the godless refuse to obey. The neutral reading clarifies that 'with difficulty' (molis) refers to the experiential ardor of the journey, not uncertainty about God's ability to save, but the difficulty itself implies that human endurance through trial is a real and necessary element of the salvation process.
key_phrases: it is time for judgment to begin with the household of God
what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God
if it is with difficulty that the righteous is saved, what will become of the godless man and the sinner

sections.section_title: Entrusting the Soul to a Faithful Creator
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that those who suffer according to God's will are to entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while continuing to do what is right, modeling the same posture of self-entrustment that Christ demonstrated on the cross.
sections.relevance: The passage presents entrustment to God as a genuine human act, not as passive resignation or a state imposed by decree. The neutral reading emphasizes that the entrustment is 'not passive resignation or fatalistic withdrawal from life' but 'active trust expressed through continued good conduct.' The community must choose to entrust, and this choosing is paired with ongoing right action ('in doing what is right'). God is 'faithful' (pistos) -- he is trustworthy -- but the community must exercise faith (pistis) toward him. The correspondence between divine faithfulness and human trust presupposes that both are genuine: God genuinely keeps his commitments, and humans genuinely choose to rely on him.
key_phrases: entrust their souls to a faithful Creator in doing what is right
suffer according to the will of God
